passage: Yusuf sits behind me in Class 4, and I've watched his face all term. During the poetry recital he had the same calm face as during the fire drill and when he got his art prize. Some kids say he's always cross, but when I asked him if something was wrong, he looked surprised and said, "No, I'm just listening." Later, when the bell rang for games, he smiled a lot and ran off. So I don't think that flat look means anything bad. It's just how his face rests. Reena keeps trying to work out if he's upset, and I keep telling her, ask him, don't guess.

qa.q: Where does Yusuf sit in relation to the narrator?
qa.a: Yusuf sits behind the narrator in Class 4.

qa.q: What did Yusuf mean when he said "I'm just listening", and what mistaken reading did other kids have?
qa.a: He meant his calm face showed he was paying attention, not that he was upset. Some kids read the flat look as being cross.

qa.q: What could Reena do instead of guessing Yusuf's mood?
qa.a: She could ask him directly, or watch how he acts over time, like when he smiles at games, before deciding anything.

qa.q: How might Reena feel about Yusuf's flat look?
qa.a: Reena may stay unsure and keep worrying that Yusuf is upset, because she tries to work it out from his face instead of asking him.

grounding: A child with a calm resting face is neither happy nor sad, and adults and peers should not over-read a neutral face.

passage:
Monday. Sarita, seven, came to Vijay's Class 3 with a calm still face and sat in the corner. Vijay wondered if she was sad. He asked, "Are you okay?" She nodded. She stayed calm during the story hour.

Wednesday. Vijay noticed Sarita's face the same during art, but her hands were busily drawing a bright kite. He decided not to guess and just said, "That's a lovely kite." Sarita said, "It's for Diwali."

Friday. When the class clapped for her drawing, Sarita's face stayed calm, but she said "thank you" warmly. Vijay realised the calm face was simply hers. He stopped worrying and just talked.

qa.q: What did Sarita draw on Wednesday?
qa.a: She drew a bright kite.

qa.q: What was Vijay wondering about Sarita's calm face at first, and what changed his mind?
qa.a: He wondered if she was sad. After seeing her busy drawing, hearing about the Diwali kite and her warm thank you, he realised the calm face was just how she looks.

qa.q: What could a teacher do with a child who has a neutral face?
qa.a: Avoid guessing from the face, offer simple friendly comments, and pay attention to what the child says and does.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel when Vijay asked if she was okay?
qa.a: She nodded, so she may have felt fine but a bit puzzled by the question. Her calm face did not show that she was content.

grounding: A child with a calm resting face is neither happy nor sad, and a teacher over several days learns not to over-read it.

passage: Thursday. Science class was so hard today! Mr Iyer's chair squeaked when he sat, and it sounded like a duck. My whole body wanted to laugh. Suraj looked at me and I nearly burst. I pressed my lips together, bit my cheek and looked at my shoes. My shoulders were shaking. I held on until the bell, and then ran outside and laughed and laughed until I got hiccups. Suraj did too. It's hard, holding it in, but I know that class is not the place to laugh loudly. I felt proud that I did it, but I was also dying to let go. 😄 — Naveen

qa.q: What did the chair sound like?
qa.a: It sounded like a duck.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling during science class, and how do you know?
qa.a: Naveen was amused and trying to hold it in, with shaking shoulders and a bitten cheek. Naveen also felt proud of that control.

qa.q: What could Naveen do to release the energy afterwards?
qa.a: Naveen can run and laugh outside at break, as before, or share the joke with Suraj once class is over.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel on catching Naveen's eye?
qa.a: Suraj looked at Naveen and probably felt the same urge to laugh, and their eye contact made it harder for both.

grounding: A child holds in laughter in class using self-control, then releases the energy afterwards.

passage: At the village school in Kotra, the Class 4 children sat in a row on the mat waiting for their turn to read from the big book. Zeenat was seventh in line. She hopped her fingers on her knee and watched the others, whispering the words with her lips. Tanuja, the teacher, saw her and smiled. When the boy before Zeenat stumbled over a word, she almost blurted out the answer, and pressed her hand to her mouth instead. She waited until Tanuja nodded, and then read the whole page in one go. After school she ran three times around the banyan tree, shouting, and Tanuja watched her from the door.

qa.q: What place in line was Zeenat?
qa.a: Zeenat was seventh in line.

qa.q: How was Zeenat feeling when she pressed her hand to her mouth, and why did she wait?
qa.a: She was eager, almost bursting to say the word when the boy stumbled, but she held back to wait for her own turn, which shows growing self-control.

qa.q: What could adults do to help children who have to wait a lot?
qa.a: They can give chances to move and release energy afterwards, like running around the tree, as Zeenat did.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see Zeenat's behaviour in class and afterwards?
qa.a: Tanuja sees a child using restraint during class and needing to run afterwards. Tanuja smiles while watching, so seems to understand.

grounding: A child waits for her turn and holds back an answer, using self-control, then needs to release energy afterwards.

passage: Sunday, late. I've been sick with fever all week, and today was the first day I went to school. Everything felt heavy, even my bag. I walked so slowly that Parveen had to wait at the gate twice. In the class my eyes kept closing and when Rohit asked me for my ruler, I snapped, "Get your own!" I felt bad right after. Amma says I need lots of sleep and no big homework for a few days. She made khichdi and let me lie on the sofa. I feel a little better now. If I'm still this tired next week, Amma says we'll ask the doctor. — Imran

qa.q: Who waited at the gate twice for Imran?
qa.a: Parveen waited at the gate twice.

qa.q: Why did Imran snap at Rohit, and what does Imran say about feeling afterwards?
qa.a: Imran was worn out after being ill, so snapped easily. Imran felt bad right after, which shows the snap was tiredness and not meanness.

qa.q: What could Imran's family do to help Imran recover?
qa.a: Give Imran rest and low demands, as Amma does, and check with the doctor if the tiredness goes on.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel about waiting for Imran?
qa.a: Parveen waited at the gate twice, so is probably patient and caring, and might also be worried about how slow and heavy Imran looks.

grounding: A school-age child after illness looks drained, moves slowly and snaps easily; weariness needs rest and low demands, and lasting exhaustion calls for checking health.

passage: The harvest week at Amandeep's family farm went on until dark every day. Chandrika, ten, had helped carry sacks since morning. By the fifth evening she was moving as if underwater, dragging her feet and rubbing her eyes. Amandeep, her cousin, asked her to fetch the water pail and she snapped, "You do it, I'm tired!" He looked surprised. Chandrika sat on the step and put her chin in her hands. Her mother saw her and said, "Enough for today. Eat, then sleep." Chandrika didn't argue. Later Amandeep brought her a glass of milk and didn't say anything about the snap.

qa.q: What did Chandrika drag as she moved?
qa.a: She dragged her feet.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika snap at Amandeep, and what else could be behind her reaction?
qa.a: She was tired after days of work and snapped without meaning to. If this tiredness kept up, it might point to something else, like sleep or stress, that needs a check.

qa.q: What could the family do to help Chandrika after the harvest week?
qa.a: Let her rest with fewer chores, make sure she gets enough sleep, and check with a doctor if the tiredness lasts.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel after Chandrika's snap?
qa.a: He was surprised but brought her milk and said nothing, so he seems to understand she was worn out.

grounding: A school-age child after long days of work looks drained, moves slowly and snaps easily; rest and low demands help.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Monday. In the school corridor, Ramesh's friend Jatin went pale when he saw the notice board with the results. Ramesh laughed and said, "Scared?" Jatin's lips were tight and he said nothing.

Wednesday. During assembly in the hot sun, Jatin's face went white again, he swayed and his hands felt cold. Ramesh held his arm and said, "Sit down." A teacher brought water and asked him to rest.

Friday. Jatin's mother took him to the doctor. He was fine, just skipping breakfast. He told Ramesh, "Monday was fear, Wednesday was the sun and no food." Ramesh nodded. "Now I know to ask."

qa.q: What did Ramesh do when Jatin swayed at assembly?
qa.a: He held Jatin's arm and told him to sit down.

qa.q: What could Jatin's pale face on Monday and Wednesday have meant, and how did they turn out?
qa.a: Monday's paleness came from fear about the results, while Wednesday's came from the hot sun and no breakfast. The same look had two different causes.

qa.q: What should someone do when a friend goes pale and dizzy?
qa.a: Help them sit down, get water and call an adult, as Ramesh and the teacher did.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt when he said "Scared?" and later saw Jatin sway?
qa.a: He may have felt guilty for joking and worried when Jatin swayed. His "Now I know to ask" suggests he learned to check first.

grounding: A child who goes pale may be scared, ill or faint, and sudden paleness with dizziness needs sitting down, water and adult help.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Pallavi, listen. When I was your age, at my school near Kochi, my friend Himani went pale in the middle of the test. I thought she'd seen a ghost. Her lips were grey and she was blinking slowly. "Are you scared?" I whispered. She said, "I feel strange." I put my hand up and called the teacher. The teacher sat Himani down and gave her water, and they took her to the nurse. It turned out she had skipped breakfast and the room was very stuffy. I've never forgotten that day. From it I learnt that a pale face has many stories and the first thing to do is sit the person down and get an adult.

qa.q: What did Himani say when asked if she was scared?
qa.a: She said, "I feel strange."

qa.q: What did Himani's pale face and slow blinking suggest, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: It suggested she might be scared or unwell, and it turned out she skipped breakfast in a stuffy room. The face alone could not tell the cause.

qa.q: What could a student do if a classmate goes pale in the middle of a test?
qa.a: Tell the teacher straight away, as the narrator did, and help the classmate sit down and get water.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt as the teacher and nurse helped her?
qa.a: She said she felt strange, so she was probably unsure and unsteady, and likely relieved to have adults help.

grounding: An elder recalls a classmate who went pale for reasons other than fear, and the need to sit down, drink water and involve an adult.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Tuesday evening. Today was the maths test and my hands were slippery and my forehead was wet. Neelam sat next to me and whispered, "Are you hot?" I said, "A bit." Actually the fan wasn't working, and also I was very scared about fractions. After the test I ran to the playground for football and sweated even more, but that felt good, not scary. Amma says sweat can mean lots of things, and you have to look at where you are and how you feel. At night I had no fever, so it was just a hot day and nerves. I'll do better next time. — Gargi

qa.q: Why was the fan not helping in the classroom?
qa.a: The fan wasn't working.

qa.q: What might have made Gargi sweat during the test, and how did Gargi tell the difference from football?
qa.a: The hot room and fear about fractions both could have made Gargi sweat. Sweating at football felt good and not scary, so the setting and Gargi's feelings helped tell them apart.

qa.q: What could Gargi do next time Gargi gets nervous before a test?
qa.a: Gargi could breathe slowly and tell someone about feeling nervous, and remember that sweat alone doesn't tell the cause.

qa.q: How might Neelam have seen Gargi's sweating?
qa.a: Neelam asked "Are you hot?", so Neelam guessed it was the heat. Neelam may not have known Gargi was also scared.

grounding: A child sweats from heat, exercise and nervousness before a test; the cause cannot be told from sweat alone, so the setting and other signs matter.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: On the sports day at the village school, Harsha's face was dripping by the time the relay ended. Gargi, the PT teacher, looked at him. It was noon in the hot dusty field and he'd just run. She didn't think much. Later in class, Harsha sweated again while sitting still, and his hands kept turning the corner of his notebook. She recalled that the maths test began in ten minutes. She asked, "Are you all right?" He said, "A bit nervous." Gargi nodded and told him to take a sip of water and a slow breath. She knew the same sweat could mean heat, running or nerves.

qa.q: What did Harsha do with his notebook while sweating in class?
qa.a: His hands kept turning the corner of his notebook.

qa.q: Why did Gargi treat Harsha's sweat at noon differently from the sweat in class, and what was Harsha feeling in class?
qa.a: At noon he had just run in the heat, so the setting explained it. In class he was still and fidgeting before the test, and he said he was nervous.

qa.q: What could Gargi do to help Harsha before the test?
qa.a: Have him take a sip of water and a slow breath, and keep checking in, as she did.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel about being asked if he is all right?
qa.a: He answered honestly that he was nervous, so he may feel relieved that his teacher noticed instead of assuming.

grounding: A school-age child sweats from heat, exercise and nervousness before a test, and the teacher reads the setting and other signs.

passage: "Yogesh, hold your horses," said Dhruv's father to the boys running in the flat corridor. Dhruv stopped and looked at the ground. "What horses?" he whispered to Yogesh. Yogesh shrugged. At school the next day Yogesh asked the teacher, "What does 'hold your horses' mean?" She smiled and said it means slow down and wait. Yogesh told Dhruv at recess. "Also, when Papa says 'you're pulling my leg,' it means joking." Dhruv laughed. "So no horses and no legs?" They tried it on each other all week, saying things like "Don't spill the beans!" and giggling.

qa.q: What did Dhruv's father say to the boys in the corridor?
qa.a: He said, "Yogesh, hold your horses."

qa.q: What was Dhruv thinking and feeling when he looked at the ground and whispered about horses, and what did Yogesh do?
qa.a: Dhruv was confused about the phrase and thought it might be literal. Yogesh asked the teacher what it meant, which is a good habit.

qa.q: What could the boys do when they hear an idiom they do not know?
qa.a: Ask an adult or friend what it means, as Yogesh did, and try it out in a fun way.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's father see the boys' reaction?
qa.a: He probably meant it lightly or as politeness and may find it funny that they took it literally.

grounding: A child learns idioms and asks what someone meant, showing asking is a good habit; indirect speech may show humour or politeness.

passage:
"Papa, Aunty Meena said it's a piece of cake." Hemant put his fork down.
"What is?" asked Raghav.
"The exam. But she's not giving cake."
Raghav laughed. "It means it's easy."
"So why not say easy?"
"People like fun ways to say things. Also, sometimes it's polite. If your friend says 'I might come if I can,' what could that mean?"
Hemant thought. "Maybe no?"
"Maybe. Or maybe they're really unsure. What would you do?"
"Ask," said Hemant. "'Do you want to come?'"
"Good habit." 🙂

qa.q: What did Aunty Meena say about the exam?
qa.a: She said it's a piece of cake.

qa.q: Why did Hemant feel puzzled about the piece of cake, and what did Hemant decide to do about 'I might come if I can'?
qa.a: Hemant was confused about why she didn't say easy. Hemant decided to ask directly to find out what a friend meant.

qa.q: What could Hemant do the next time he hears a hint or figure of speech?
qa.a: Ask what the person means, kindly and directly, as Hemant planned to.

qa.q: How might Aunty Meena have meant her piece of cake?
qa.a: She may have meant it as a friendly, encouraging joke to help Hemant feel less nervous about the exam.

grounding: A child learns idioms and hints, and asks what someone meant; indirect speech can show humour or politeness.

passage: At Jahnavi's birthday party at the community hall, everyone lined up for the group photo. Akash, who I sit next to in class, was in the front row and shouted "Cheese!" with the biggest smile. I clapped for him. But when I looked at a candid shot later, he had his chin on his hand and heavy eyes, staring at the cake, not smiling at all. Jahnavi said, "He looks bored!" I wasn't sure. Akash had been up since 5 am for his early cricket practice. The two photos told different stories, but neither one told me what he really felt. I asked him later, and he just yawned.

qa.q: What did Akash shout for the group photo?
qa.a: He shouted "Cheese!"

qa.q: What did Akash's smile in the posed photo and heavy eyes in the candid shot each suggest, and what was the likely reason?
qa.a: The posed smile shows he cooperated for the photo, and the heavy eyes suggest tiredness, maybe from early cricket practice. Jahnavi read it as boredom, so another reading was possible.

qa.q: What could the narrator do to find out how Akash felt?
qa.a: Ask him kindly rather than guessing from a photo, as the narrator did.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see the candid photo of Akash?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees a bored-looking guest at the party and may feel a little hurt, without knowing he was tired.

grounding: A child says cheese and smiles for a photo but looks tired in a candid moment, and a posed smile shows cooperation, not necessarily feeling.

passage:
Day one. At the family wedding, Bhavna, ten, posed for the photographer with a wide smile beside Kunal, her cousin. The flashes lit them up, and she said "Cheese!" with everyone.

Day two. Kunal saw a candid photo of Bhavna on the phone: her eyes were half closed, a hand on her cheek. "You look tired," he said. She nodded. "Very. The dancing went until midnight."

Day three. Kunal looked at both photos again. "In one you look happy and in the other sleepy," he said. Bhavna grinned. "Both are me. The first is for the album."

qa.q: How late did the dancing go?
qa.a: The dancing went until midnight.

qa.q: What did each of the two photos of Bhavna show about how she felt?
qa.a: The posed photo shows her cooperating with a wide smile, while the candid one shows tiredness after late dancing. Neither photo alone gives the full picture.

qa.q: What could Kunal do to understand a cousin better than photos allow?
qa.a: Ask how she feels, as he did, and remember that photos show only a moment.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel about the two photos?
qa.a: She says "Both are me", so she sees both as true in different ways and seems comfortable, if tired.

grounding: A child smiles for a posed photo but looks tired in a candid moment; the posed smile shows cooperation and both images tell different stories.

passage: Wednesday. Today at dinner Papa was very quiet, and I noticed his voice was lower when he asked me to pass the salt. His eyebrows were a tiny bit closer together than usual. I got worried: did I do something? I thought about my maths test and the broken cup. Gopika, my sister, didn't notice anything. After dinner I said, "Papa, are you okay?" He looked surprised and said, "Just tired from work, beta. Not about you." I felt my shoulders come down. I'm glad I asked and didn't just guess, because I might have gotten so worried for nothing. — Sangeeta

qa.q: What did Sangeeta's father say when Sangeeta asked if he was okay?
qa.a: He said, "Just tired from work, beta. Not about you."

qa.q: What did Sangeeta think when she noticed her father's lower voice and closer eyebrows, and what did Sangeeta do about it?
qa.a: Sangeeta worried about having done something wrong, but asked him instead of guessing. His answer showed the cue meant tiredness.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do the next time she notices a small change in a parent?
qa.a: Check quickly and kindly by asking, as before, so the cue is not over-read or missed.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Sangeeta asks if he is okay?
qa.a: He looked surprised, so he may not have realised Sangeeta noticed. He may feel touched and reassure Sangeeta.

grounding: A child notices subtle signals such as a lower voice and slight frown in a parent, and a short check keeps the reading honest.

passage: The evening bus to Lakshmi's village was late, and her mother, Sangeeta, sat in the seat next to her. Lakshmi looked sideways at her mother. Her mouth was a little flat and she was gripping her bag. She'd stopped talking after they passed the temple. Lakshmi wondered if it was the news from the school about her marks. She thought hard, but couldn't tell. Then she said quietly, "Amma, are you worried about something?" Sangeeta blinked. "Only my back, beta, this seat is hard. Don't you worry." Lakshmi smiled and offered her own cloth bag as a cushion. Her mother laughed.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi offer her mother as a cushion?
qa.a: She offered her own cloth bag.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi think her mother's flat mouth and grip on the bag might mean, and what did she find out?
qa.a: She wondered if her mother was worried about her marks, but Sangeeta said it was her back on a hard seat. The cue could be read in different ways.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi do when she can't tell what a small cue means?
qa.a: Ask a short, gentle question, as she did on the bus.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel about Lakshmi checking on her?
qa.a: Sangeeta blinked and then laughed, so she may feel touched to be noticed, and amused at how worried Lakshmi was.

grounding: A child notices small changes such as a flat mouth and silence in a parent, and a short check corrects over-reading.

passage: The Class 5 hall at the community school was decorated with balloons for the surprise for Maria, the class teacher, who had a birthday. Dilnaz stood by the door with a big card behind her back. Her heart was thumping, and she wanted to shout. But when Maria came in, Dilnaz kept her face perfectly plain and said, "Good morning, Ma'am," in the usual voice. Ma'am gave her a suspicious look. Dilnaz's friends were nearly bursting with laughter. Only when everybody yelled "Happy birthday!" did Dilnaz bring out the card, grinning wide. Maria laughed and said, "You had me fooled!"

qa.q: What was Dilnaz holding behind her back?
qa.a: She was holding a big card.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling while she kept her face plain, and why did she hold back?
qa.a: She was excited, with her heart thumping, and she kept her face plain to keep the surprise until the right moment. Her wide grin at the end shows the excitement was there all along.

qa.q: What could adults do to make the most of a child's kept-in excitement?
qa.a: Enjoy the delay and let the child reveal the surprise in the right moment, as Maria did by laughing along.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt on entering the room and seeing Dilnaz's plain face?
qa.a: Maria looked suspicious, so she may have sensed something was up and was curious. She then felt delighted and surprised.

grounding: A child keeps a straight face at a surprise while feeling excitement, waiting for the right moment, and the adult enjoys the delay.

passage: Manoj, who lives next door, told me what he saw. "Dhruv came back from school with the biggest smile I've ever seen, but only in his eyes. His face was calm, like a statue. I asked him how his day was and he said, 'Fine,' very serious. But his fingers kept tapping and he bounced on his toes. I thought something was up. Then his mother came out of the house and he burst out, 'I won the drawing prize!' and held up a golden ribbon. He'd been saving it for her. I said 'Congratulations,' and he grinned at me. I think he wanted it to be a surprise."

qa.q: What did Dhruv hold up when his mother came out?
qa.a: He held up a golden ribbon.

qa.q: What might Dhruv's calm face with tapping fingers have meant, and what else did Manoj consider?
qa.a: It probably meant excitement kept in until he could tell his mother. Manoj only thought something was up and could not be sure.

qa.q: What could Dhruv's mother do when she hears his news?
qa.a: Enjoy the surprise and share his excitement fully, since he had been holding it in for her.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Dhruv's behaviour?
qa.a: Manoj noticed his fingers tapping and bouncing but couldn't be sure of the reason, only guessing it was a surprise.

grounding: A child keeps a straight face at a surprise while feeling excitement, waiting for the right moment, as an observer guesses.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 6. In the games period Mridul was told by the referee that his goal was offside and would not count. Eshaan, our PT teacher, watched him say, "Okay," with clenched jaw and pressed lips, then turn and walk away, hands in fists. He did not shout or argue, which I'd like to praise. When the game ended, though, he kicked the ball hard against the wall. I took him aside and said, "I saw you keep calm and it looked hard." He said, "It wasn't fair." We talked, and he ran two laps to burn off the energy. I will follow up on how he feels about the offside rule. — Eshaan

qa.q: What did the referee say about Mridul's goal?
qa.a: The referee said the goal was offside and would not count.

qa.q: What did Mridul's clenched jaw and fists suggest he was feeling despite saying okay?
qa.a: They suggest he was angry about what felt unfair, though he held it in. Kicking the ball later shows the anger needed a way out.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do to help Mridul with anger after being polite?
qa.a: Give a safe outlet, like the laps, listen to his view, and explain the rule calmly.

qa.q: How might the referee see Mridul's reaction?
qa.a: The referee probably saw a player who accepted the decision politely and may not have noticed how angry Mridul felt.

grounding: A child says okay while angry at a rule that feels unfair; politeness shows self-control but the anger still needs a safe outlet.

passage: Thursday night. Vikas said we couldn't play cricket in the lane because the ball hit a window last week. I said, "Okay," and smiled a small smile, and went home. But inside I was fuming. It wasn't me who broke the window! Everyone else was playing too. I banged my bag on the table and Amma raised her eyebrows. I said, "I'm fine." Later I punched my pillow ten times until I felt better. Then I told Amma what happened. She said I could ask Vikas whether we can play in the park. I think I'll do that tomorrow. — Sunaina

qa.q: Who told Sunaina they couldn't play in the lane?
qa.a: Vikas told Sunaina they couldn't play cricket in the lane.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel when she said "Okay" with a small smile, and what did she do with the feeling later?
qa.a: Sunaina was angry because it seemed unfair, since Sunaina wasn't the one who broke the window. Sunaina let it out safely by punching her pillow and then talking to Amma.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do next about the cricket rule?
qa.a: Sunaina could ask Vikas calmly whether they can play in the park, as Amma suggested.

qa.q: How might Vikas see Sunaina's reply?
qa.a: Vikas heard an okay and a smile, so Vikas may think Sunaina accepted it and not know how Sunaina felt.

grounding: A child says okay politely while angry at a rule that feels unfair, and the anger needs a safe outlet afterwards.
